beliefs.practice: Use a single MongoClient/MongoClient-equivalent instance (singleton) shared across the process and threads; do not create a new client per request. Configure sensible pool sizes (maxPoolSize) and timeouts at client creation.
Never hard-code the connection string or credentials; read the DocumentDB URI and credentials from environment variables (or Azure Key Vault) and keep a .env.example with placeholders only.
Do not log full connection strings, API keys, or document contents that may contain secrets or PII. Redact or omit sensitive fields in logs and telemetry.
Create indexes idempotently at application startup (or during a migration): call create_index / create_indexes with the exact key spec and options so index creation is safe to run multiple times.

Index all fields used in frequent equality and sort/filter patterns (e.g., sku, timestamp, competitor_id, active flag). Use compound indexes for queries that filter by multiple fields together (e.g., {'sku':1,'timestamp':-1}).
Use TTL indexes (expireAfterSeconds) for time-series / metric collections (demand metrics) to automatically purge old documents and reduce storage and RU consumption.

For vector search, create and tune an ANN index (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN parameters such as M, efConstruction, efSearch) appropriate to your recall/latency tradeoff; store vectors in a dedicated field and index that field with the vector index type.
When reading documents for decision-making, use projections to fetch only required fields (e.g., price, sku, timestamp, margin rules) to reduce network and request charge.
Avoid large skip-based pagination for high offsets; prefer range-based pagination (e.g., timestamp or _id cursors) to keep queries efficient and low-cost.

Perform single-document atomic updates with find_one_and_update (with a filter) or update operators ($set, $inc). Use the operation's returned document (or returnDocument option) to confirm the write.

For cross-document or multi-collection atomic work, prefer application-level compensating transactions or explicit DB transactions only if the Mongo API and server version support them and you have tested their behavior/limits in the target DocumentDB environment.

Use optimistic concurrency control for price updates to avoid lost updates: include a version field or use a server-side optimistic check (filter by previous value or _etag) in the find-and-update filter.

Implement retry logic with exponential backoff for transient errors and rate-limited responses (HTTP 429 / Mongo-specific throttling). Respect Retry-After headers when provided and cap retries to avoid runaway loops.
Monitor request charge / RU consumption, latency, 429s, and index usage. Use those metrics to tune RU provisioning or autoscale and to optimize hot queries and indexes.

Design collection documents for query patterns: keep product and pricing data denormalized enough to read pricing decisions in a single document where practical, and store frequently-changed telemetry/metrics in separate collections to avoid document churn.
Make seed scripts idempotent: check for existing documents, use upserts or conditional inserts, and avoid destructive operations so seeding can be safely repeated against the same database.

Provision collections (containers) with an appropriate partition/shard key chosen for even distribution at scale; avoid high-cardinality hotspots on a single partition key value (e.g., avoid using a constant or low-cardinality field as the partition key).

Tune client connection options: set serverSelectionTimeoutMS, socketTimeoutMS/connectTimeoutMS, and heartbeatFrequency appropriately for your network and app needs so that operations fail fast when the DB is unreachable.

Use appropriate readConcern/readPreference and writeConcern settings consistent with your consistency needs: prefer stronger guarantees for financial/price writes and lower-latency weaker guarantees for non-critical reads if necessary.

When using LLM-based tooling in the agent, never supply raw DB keys or connection strings to the model; instrument tools so the model calls parameterized functions that perform DB queries and updates on its behalf.
